entries.answer: A stock is a small ownership share in a company, and the thing people misunderstand about it is that it is not a lottery ticket with a company name on it: the return comes from the business doing well and the price reflecting that, not from a number going up by luck. A share price moves because people are buying and selling based on what they expect, so a company doing well can still fall if people expect more, which is the difference between a business and a bet on the business. The practical consequence is that a stock held for a few years is a different proposition from one held for a few days, and most losses in investing come from treating the second as if it were the first. Diversification exists because companies fail, and the point of holding many is that one bad outcome does not sink the whole portfolio. The honest warning is that the past is not a promise: what worked in one decade may not work in the next, and anyone selling a specific return is selling something other than advice.

entries.answer: Diversification is holding investments that do not all move together, and it is the only genuinely free thing available in investing: spreading reduces the effect of any single bad outcome without lowering the expected return. The reason it works is that prices move on different drivers, so a property, a share and a cash deposit are not responding to the same piece of news on the same day. What it does not do is protect against everything, and the failure mode is a portfolio that looks varied but is not: several holdings in the same industry are one holding wearing a disguise, and the person who realises that usually does so in the same month the industry falls. It also costs a little, in fees and in the attention needed to check that the spread is still real, and for a small amount of money that cost can exceed the benefit, which is why a beginner with a few thousand pesos is often better served by one simple thing than by a complicated mix.

entries.answer: A mutual fund pools money from many people and invests it, and the reason it exists is that doing that alone is the part that is hard. One person cannot hold a broad spread of investments economically, since buying into hundreds of companies means hundreds of separate purchases, and a single share of one company is a concentrated bet that can go to nothing. The fund buys a broad set and gives each contributor a claim on the whole, so the small investor gets the diversification they could not build for themselves. What a holder owns is therefore not a company but a slice of a collection, and the usual charges are a management fee and a dealing charge, both taken before the return is passed on, so a fund that performs well can still lose to the same money in a savings account over a short period. The honest framing is that this is a way of being invested rather than a way of avoiding risk.
